0.title: Positions at a Glance
0.essay:
This page gathers, in one place, the positions this commentary and its topical studies take, from the inspiration of Scripture to the meaning of 666. Each entry gives this commentary’s view in a sentence, the main views other Christians hold, and where to read the full discussion.

Scripture

Inspiration. Scripture is God-breathed in its very words, not only its ideas; the Spirit guided the writers through their own personalities, not by mechanical dictation. Others: Some say the Bible contains God’s word in merely human words. (Where: 1 Corinthians 2; 2 Peter 1)

Inerrancy. Scripture as first given is without error in all it affirms, infallible in its teaching and sufficient for faith and life. Others: Some limit inspiration to religious teaching, or allow errors alongside truth. (Where: 2 Timothy 3; 2 Peter 1; Ecclesiastes 12)

Sufficiency and clarity. Scripture is self-authenticating, sufficient for salvation and godliness, so no further revelation is needed, and clear enough in its main teaching for ordinary believers to understand. Others: Rome holds that Scripture needs the church’s teaching office to interpret it; some treat it as a mystery for experts. (Where: The Doctrines of Grace (The Authority of Scripture); Psalm 119)

Bible translations. Use a faithful translation you will actually read: formal translations such as the ESV and NASB suit study, functional ones such as the NIV suit wide reading; no single translation is required. Others: King James-only Christians hold the KJV alone to be the faithful English Bible. (Where: How We Got Our Bible (Giving the Bible to the World; How to Read It Well))

Sola Scriptura. Scripture alone is the final authority; councils deserve respect where they agree with it, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err, and no church may bind the conscience beyond God’s word. Others: Rome and Orthodoxy hold Scripture together with apostolic tradition and an authoritative teaching office. (Where: 1 Corinthians 4; Acts 15; Acts 17; 2 Thessalonians 2; 2 Corinthians 1)

Closed canon. The canon is complete and closed: God preserved exactly the books he intended, and the Apocrypha and 1 Enoch are not Scripture, even where the New Testament mentions what they record. Others: Rome and Orthodoxy include the Maccabees; the Ethiopian church includes 1 Enoch; some groups add new scriptures. (Where: 1 Corinthians 5; Hebrews 11; Jude; Revelation 22)

New revelation. God’s speaking in his Son is final; the Spirit now illumines and applies Scripture and gives no new revelation beside it, so claimed voices, impressions and dreams must be tested by the completed word. Others: Some charismatic teaching expects continuing revelation; liberal theology finds it in experience. (Where: Hebrews 1; John 14; 1 Samuel 3; 1 Kings 19; Job 33)

Guidance. God guides chiefly through his word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel; believers should not demand signs, cast lots or steer by dreams. Others: Many seek guidance through fleeces, impressions or dreams. (Where: Genesis 24; Genesis 40; Acts 1)

Interpretation. Read for the plain meaning first, and let the New Testament’s own reading guide the Old: the promises to Abraham and David are fulfilled in Christ and his one people; Galatians 4 is typology, and parables make their main point, not a code in every detail. Others: Dispensational interpretation reads prophecy as literally as possible for national Israel; allegorical reading finds hidden meanings in details. (Where: Hermeneutics; Galatians 4; Luke 10)

Isaiah’s authorship. The whole book comes from Isaiah, chapters 40 to 66 included, written ahead of time, as the Gospels and John cite them. Others: Many scholars, including some who hold Scripture wholly true, see a later prophet. (Where: Isaiah 13; Isaiah 40)

Daniel’s date. Daniel received his visions in the sixth century BC, and God gave him real foreknowledge, while the date is openly granted to be debated. Others: Many scholars date it to the second century BC, some believing scholars on literary grounds. (Where: Daniel, Introduction; Daniel 8; Daniel 11)

Other authorship. Moses wrote the Pentateuch in substance, Deuteronomy and Leviticus included, with possible later inspired notes; Zechariah is one prophet’s work; Paul wrote Ephesians; and the psalm titles are trustworthy. Others: Many scholars see later sources, a second Zechariah, a follower of Paul, and later titles. (Where: Genesis, Introduction; Leviticus, Introduction; Deuteronomy, Introduction and 31; Zechariah, Introduction; Ephesians 1; Psalms, Introduction)

History in the Old Testament. Jonah is history, chiefly because Jesus treated it so; Job was a real man, and the book records real events shaped into poetry; Esther is a true account, Joshua’s long day a real miracle, and Nebuchadnezzar’s madness and Darius the Mede real history. Others: Some read these books or episodes as parable, drama or legend. (Where: Jonah 1; Job 1; Esther, Introduction; Joshua 10; Daniel 4; Daniel 5)

The end of Mark. Mark 16:9–20 was most likely added early, probably in the second century; whether Mark meant to end at 16:8 is less certain. Others: Some hold the longer ending original; others think the true ending was lost. (Where: Mark 16)

John 7:53–8:11. The account of the woman caught in adultery was not part of John’s original Gospel, though it may record a true event; no doctrine should rest on it alone. Others: Some, with the later manuscripts behind the KJV, hold it original. (Where: John 8)

Text and canon: smaller verdicts. Many single-verse calls follow the earliest manuscripts, adding that no doctrine depends on them: Matthew 17:21, 18:11 and 23:14 are not original, while nor the Son in Matthew 24:36 is; differing numbers between Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah are copying slips, not errors in Scripture as first given; and alleged errors such as Abiathar (Mark 2:26) dissolve on careful reading. Others: KJV readers often prefer the longer readings; some scholars count such details as slips. (Where: for example Matthew 17, 23, 24; Mark 2; 2 Samuel 8; 1 Chronicles, Introduction; Ezra 2; Nehemiah 7)

God

The Trinity. One God who exists eternally as three persons, each fully God: not one person in three modes, not three gods, and the Son no creature; every illustration fails somewhere, so it is wiser to stay close to Scripture’s words. Others: Modalists (common through the water illustration) make the persons roles; Arians and Jehovah’s Witnesses make the Son a creature; tritheism makes three gods. (Where: The Trinity (Three Persons; Guarding the Truth); Genesis 1; 1 Corinthians 8)

The deity of Christ. Jesus is fully God: the Word was God, not a god; he is called God in Romans 9:5, Titus 2:13 and 1 John 5:20; and firstborn and beginning mean supremacy and source, not that he was created. Others: Arians and Jehovah’s Witnesses make the Son a created being. (Where: John 1; John 8; Colossians 1; Titus 2; Revelation 3)

The Son’s submission. The Son’s submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook as Mediator, not to any subordination of his being. Others: Some argue for an eternal order of authority and submission within the Godhead. (Where: 1 Corinthians 11; 1 Corinthians 15; John 14)

Eternal generation and procession. The persons are distinguished by eternal relations: the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son (the filioque, right in substance); the three work inseparably, the Father planning, the Son accomplishing and the Spirit applying salvation. Others: The Orthodox reject the filioque; some deny eternal generation. (Where: The Trinity (Three Persons; The Trinity and Our Salvation); John 15)

The Holy Spirit as God. The Spirit is a distinct person, fully God and rightly worshipped, not a divine energy; the seven spirits of Revelation 1:4 are the Spirit in his fullness. Others: Some see the Spirit as an impersonal force; some take the seven spirits as angels. (Where: The Holy Spirit (Who the Holy Spirit Is); 2 Corinthians 3; Revelation 1)

Wisdom in Proverbs 8. It is a poetic personification of God’s wisdom, fully embodied in Christ, not a statement about the Son’s origin. Others: Some read it as a direct description of the eternal Son. (Where: Biblical Wisdom (Christ, the Wisdom of God))

The angel of the LORD. The angel who speaks and acts as God (and the commander in Joshua 5, the visitor in Judges and the glorious figure of Daniel 10) is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation. Others: Some see a created angel speaking for God. (Where: Exodus 3; Genesis 16; Daniel 3; Joshua 5; Judges 2, 6, 13; Daniel 10)

Love and wrath. God’s wrath is personal and real, the reaction of his holiness to evil; God is love does not mean his love overrides his holiness and justice; when he is said to regret, Scripture speaks in human terms. Others: Some set love against wrath; open theists say God changes his plans. (Where: Romans 1; 1 John 4; Genesis 6)

Sovereignty and providence. God ordains whatever comes to pass, including sinful acts and hardened hearts, without being the author of sin; his decretive will (what he ordains) differs from his preceptive will (what he commands), and his decree includes the means, so human choices and prayers are real. Others: Arminians hold that God permits but does not ordain sin and free choices. (Where: The Doctrines of Grace (The Sovereignty of God); Ephesians 1; Genesis 45; Exodus 9; Acts 27; Isaiah 10)

Providence. God preserves all things, works in and through his creatures’ actions (concurrence) and governs all to his ends, usually through ordinary means; providence is neither deism nor chance. Others: Deists picture a watchmaker who walked away; many speak of luck or chance. (Where: The Providence of God (What Providence Is); Esther)

Free will. Fallen people are free in that nothing forces their will, yet they are morally unable to turn to God, because the will is enslaved to what the heart loves; true freedom is the liberty to do what we truly desire, which God gives. Others: Arminian and Wesleyan Christians (for example Roger Olson) hold that God gives all people grace that restores a power of contrary choice; Erasmus defended a free will able to incline to God. (Where: The Doctrines of Grace (The Sovereignty of God; Total Depravity))

Evil and suffering. Evil and suffering fall under God’s hand without his doing evil, as the cross shows; hard providences are never a verdict on the sufferer, and God may have morally sufficient reasons we cannot see. Others: Some say God merely permits evil he does not ordain; open theists say he cannot know or prevent it; Job’s friends read suffering as punishment. (Where: The Providence of God (Hard Providences); Apologetics (The Problem of Evil); Job 1)

Creation and humanity

Six days. God created all things in six ordinary days: each is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel’s week in God’s. Others: Faithful Christians also hold day-age, framework and analogical-day views, an old earth, or creation through evolution. (Where: Genesis 1; Creation & the Fall (Six Days); Exodus 20; Psalm 90; Proverbs 8)

A young creation. The genealogies are true history, perhaps with small gaps, and with the six days point to a young creation, with no ruin-and-gap before Genesis 1:2 and no death before the fall. Others: Many faithful Christians hold an old earth; Ussher dated creation to 4004 BC. (Where: Genesis 1; Genesis 5; Psalm 104)

Adam and Eve. Adam and Eve were real people, specially created, from whom all humanity descends; Paul’s argument in Romans 5 needs a real Adam. Others: Theistic evolution often treats Adam as a representative figure. (Where: Genesis 2; Acts 17; Romans 5)

The fall. The fall was a real event that brought sin and death into the world, and it is also every person’s story. Others: Some read it only as a symbol. (Where: Genesis 3)

The covenant of works. Adam stood under a covenant of works as humanity’s representative head, as Christ is the head of his people. Others: Some object that the word covenant is not used. (Where: Genesis 2)

Original sin. All sinned in Adam: his guilt is counted to the whole race, and all are born guilty and corrupt. Others: Pelagians say Adam only set a bad example. (Where: Romans 5; Ephesians 2)

Total depravity. Sin corrupts every part of human nature, so the natural person cannot understand the things of the Spirit or submit to God; not that people are as bad as they could be. Others: Others hold that fallen people can still freely turn to God. (Where: Ephesians 2; Romans 3; 1 Corinthians 2)

The image of God. Humans represent and reflect God in rule, relationship, reason and moral nature, men and women equally; the image is damaged by the fall, not lost. Others: Some say the image was lost at the fall. (Where: Genesis 1)

Body and soul. A human is a unity of body and soul, with soul and spirit used interchangeably. Others: Trichotomists see three parts: spirit, soul and body. (Where: 1 Thessalonians 5; Hebrews 4)

The flood. The flood was a real judgement on the world, told in universal language; its extent is left to good conscience. Others: Some hold a worldwide flood, others a regional one. (Where: Genesis 6)

Christ

The virgin birth. The virgin birth is historical fact and essential Christian doctrine. Others: Liberal theology treats it as legend. (Where: Matthew 1)

Two natures. The Son lost no divine attribute in becoming man; he emptied himself by taking human nature and a servant’s role, one person, fully God and fully man. Others: Kenotic theories say he laid aside attributes such as omniscience. (Where: Philippians 2; 2 Corinthians 8)

Could Jesus have sinned? The Son could not sin, because he is God, yet his temptations were entirely real. Others: Some argue that if he could not sin, his temptations were not real. (Where: Hebrews 4; Luke 4; Matthew 4)

Mary. Mary was a sinner saved by grace, highly favoured, a model of faith who points to her Son; the doctrine behind Mother of God is true of Christ, but she is no source of grace or mediator, and she bore other children. Others: Roman Catholic teaching holds her sinless, ever-virgin and able to intercede. (Where: Luke 1; John 2; Mark 6; Revelation 12)

Penal substitution. At the heart of the cross Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place, turning God’s wrath away; example and victory flow from it. Others: Some put moral example or victory over evil at the centre; some say the cross cleanses sin but does not turn away wrath. (Where: Ephesians 1; John 19; 1 Corinthians 15; Romans 3)

For whom did Christ die? Definite atonement: Christ died to save those the Father gave him, and his death actually accomplishes their redemption, sufficient for all and efficient for the elect, so the gospel can be offered to anyone without reservation; world and all usually mean people of every kind. Others: Arminians hold that Christ died equally for all; Amyraldians and hypothetical universalists such as Davenant hold a modified view. (Where: The Doctrines of Grace (Definite Atonement); 1 John 2; John 10; Hebrews 2; Isaiah 53)

Once for all. Christ’s sacrifice is complete, never repeated or added to; the Supper is no sacrifice and the Lord’s Table no altar. Others: Roman Catholic teaching holds the Mass to be a sacrifice. (Where: Hebrews 7; Hebrews 10; Hebrews 13; Colossians 1)

The spirits in prison. In 1 Peter 3:19 the risen Christ most likely proclaimed his triumph over fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day, held without dogmatism; it offers no second chance after death. Others: Others hold that Christ preached through Noah to his generation. (Where: 1 Peter 3; The Bible Book by Book (1 Peter))

The resurrection. Christ rose bodily, with flesh and bones and the marks of his wounds; his body is the pattern of ours. Others: Some speak of a spiritual resurrection only. (Where: Luke 24; 1 Corinthians 15)

Christ’s present reign. Christ already reigns on David’s throne at the Father’s right hand. Others: Dispensationalists expect his Davidic reign to begin in a future millennium. (Where: Acts 2; Luke 1; Luke 19; Psalm 110)

Salvation

Unconditional election. God chose individuals in Christ before the world began, freely, not for foreseen faith; his foreknowledge is his loving choice of persons, and faith is the fruit of election. Others: Arminians root election in foreseen faith; some say God chose only Christ and the church as a group. (Where: Ephesians 1; Romans 8; Romans 9; Malachi 1; The Doctrines of Grace (Unconditional Election))

Those not chosen. God passes by the rest and ordains them to wrath for their sin, without being the author of it. Others: Some deny any such decree; hyper-Calvinists say God causes their sin as he causes faith. (Where: Romans 9)

Effectual calling. God’s inward call to his chosen people does not fail: the dead need resurrection, not assistance; the outward call is resisted every day, but the Spirit’s new birth renews the will so that people come freely; regeneration comes before faith, and faith is God’s gift. Others: Arminians hold that God gives all people grace that each may accept or resist. (Where: The Grace of God (Saving Grace); The Doctrines of Grace (Irresistible Grace); John 6; Ephesians 2)

The free offer. The gospel is offered freely and sincerely to everyone; God truly calls all who hear and grieves over their refusal, yet his saving purpose never fails. Others: Hyper-Calvinists deny a sincere offer to all; Arminians infer equal grace for all. (Where: Revelation 22; Romans 10; Matthew 23; 1 Timothy 2)

Justification by faith alone. Justification is God’s once-for-all legal declaration that the believing sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted to him, received by faith alone; no one can merit anything. Others: Roman Catholic teaching includes inner renewal and good works in justification. (Where: Galatians 2; Romans 3; Philippians 3; Titus 3; Luke 17)

The New Perspective. Works of the law include the Jewish boundary markers, as the New Perspective rightly sees, but Paul’s deeper question is how a sinner is right with God, and his phrase means faith in Christ. Others: New Perspective scholars make justification mainly about who belongs to God’s people; some read the faithfulness of Christ. (Where: Galatians 2; Romans 3)

Paul and James. They do not contradict: Paul opposes earning acceptance, James opposes faith with no fruit; works show that faith is real. Others: Rome uses James to include works in justification. (Where: James 2; Genesis 22)

Christ alone. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ alone; creation leaves people without excuse, not with a way of salvation. Others: Inclusivists hold that some may be saved through Christ without hearing of him; pluralists see many ways. (Where: Matthew 7; Acts 4; Acts 14; Romans 1)

Infants who die. Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (Westminster and 1689, 10.3), and grieving parents may rest their little ones in God’s hands with real hope. Others: Many Reformed pastors hold that all who die in infancy are elect; others leave it open. (Where: 1 Corinthians 1; Acts 3; 2 Samuel 12; Death, Dying & Heaven (Grieving with Hope))

Universalism. Not all will be saved: uniting all things means bringing all under Christ’s rule, and every knee will bow, but not all willingly. Others: Universalists, from Origen on, expect all to be reconciled. (Where: Ephesians 1; Colossians 1; Philippians 2; 1 Timothy 4)

No second chance. Death fixes a person’s destiny, and judgement follows it. Others: Some read 1 Peter 3–4 as the gospel preached to the dead. (Where: Hebrews 9; 1 Peter 4; 1 Corinthians 15)

Perseverance. Those God has truly saved are kept by his power and will never finally perish. Others: Arminians hold that a true believer can finally fall away. (Where: John 6; John 10; Romans 8; Philippians 1; 1 John 2; Numbers 14)

Warning passages. The warnings are real and are God’s means of keeping his people; those who finally fall away shared the church’s outward blessings but were never regenerate. Others: Others read them as true believers losing salvation, as hypothetical, or as loss of rewards. (Where: Hebrews 6; Hebrews 10; Galatians 5; Romans 11)

Assurance. Believers can and should be assured, resting first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the Spirit’s witness and a changed life; assurance is not of the essence of faith, so a true believer may lack it for a time, and special experiences are a gift, not the test. Others: Some say never doubt; others make constant introspection the mark of faith; some urge seeking a direct sealing. (Where: 1 John 5; Romans 8; Assurance of Salvation; The Doctrines of Grace (Perseverance of the Saints))

Unforgivable sin and sin to death. Both describe a final, hardened rejection of Christ, not a single act or a list of mortal sins; anyone afraid he has committed it has not. Others: Some name a specific act such as suicide; Rome distinguishes mortal and venial sins. (Where: Luke 12; 1 John 5)

The carnal Christian. There is no permanent, acceptable class of carnal Christians, and no higher class either: one standard of discipleship applies to all. Others: Some teach that one may have Christ as Saviour but not as Lord; Rome has counsels of perfection. (Where: 1 Corinthians 3; Matthew 19)

Believers judged by works. Believers will not be condemned, but their lives will be revealed and their works rewarded by grace. Others: Some think any judgement of believers contradicts justification. (Where: 2 Corinthians 5; Romans 2)

The Holy Spirit

Baptism in the Spirit. Every believer is baptised in the Spirit at conversion and then filled again and again; there is no second baptism and no second class of Christian. Others: Pentecostal and charismatic teaching sees a later Spirit baptism, usually shown by tongues. (Where: The Holy Spirit (The Spirit Within Us); 1 Corinthians 12; John 7; Ephesians 5)

Pentecost and the delays in Acts. Pentecost was unique and unrepeatable, and the delays in Acts 8 and 19 mark the gospel crossing new boundaries, not a pattern for every believer. Others: Pentecostals see a two-stage pattern; Rome finds a basis for confirmation. (Where: Acts 2; Acts 8; Acts 19)

Cessationism. The revelatory and sign gifts attested the apostles and ceased once the foundation was laid; this is held charitably, and does not rest on 1 Corinthians 13:10, whose perfect is most likely Christ’s return. Others: Continuationists, such as Grudem and Carson, hold that all the gifts continue. (Where: The Holy Spirit (The Gifts of the Spirit); Denominations (Pentecostal & Charismatic); 1 Corinthians 12–14; Ephesians 2; Numbers 11; 2 Kings 4; Daniel 2; Isaiah 28)

Prophecy today. Prophecy as new revelation belonged to the foundation; what continues from Joel 2 is the Spirit poured on all believers, who speak God’s completed word, and claims to speak new words from God would add to Scripture. Others: Many continuationists hold a fallible prophecy, tested by Scripture. (Where: 1 Thessalonians 5; Romans 12; Joel 2; Deuteronomy 18)

Tongues. Tongues were real languages the speaker had not learned; not all spoke them, Romans 8’s groanings are not tongues, and churches should neither mock nor exclude those who believe they continue. Others: Many see tongues as ecstatic speech or a private prayer language. (Where: 1 Corinthians 14; Acts 2; Romans 8; Jude)

Healing. God heals in answer to prayer, but not always; healing now is not guaranteed by the atonement, and no one today can heal at will. Others: Healing and word-of-faith teachers say healing is guaranteed to enough faith. (Where: 2 Corinthians 12; 1 Peter 2; James 5)

The Church

Church government. Each local church is led by a plurality of qualified elders (elder and overseer are one office), with deacons serving and the congregation involved in key decisions; churches rightly cooperate. Others: Episcopal, presbyterian and congregational government; some churches have a single pastor. (Where: The Church (Elders and Deacons); 1 Timothy 3; Philippians 1)

Christ alone the head. Peter was the first confessing apostle and a foundation stone, but fallible and without successors; true succession is in doctrine, so there is no papacy. Others: Rome gives Peter a primacy passed to the bishops of Rome; Orthodox and some Anglicans hold apostolic succession. (Where: Matthew 16; John 21; Galatians 2; 2 Timothy 2)

Priesthood of all believers. Every believer is a priest; ministers are elders, not priests, and ordination is the church’s recognition and commissioning, not a sacrament. Others: Rome and Orthodoxy keep a sacrificing priesthood and sacramental ordination. (Where: 1 Peter 2; Hebrews 5; 1 Timothy 4)

Two ordinances. Christ gave two ordinances, baptism and the Lord’s Supper; marriage, anointing the sick and footwashing are not sacraments. Others: Rome counts seven; some churches keep footwashing as an ordinance. (Where: Ephesians 5; James 5; John 13)

Who should be baptised. Believers only (1689 Confession): the new covenant is made with those who know the Lord, and every New Testament baptism follows faith; paedobaptists are honoured brothers. Others: Paedobaptists baptise the infants of believers. (Where: The Church (Baptism); Covenant Theology (Covenant Theology and Baptism); Acts 2; Acts 16)

Mode and rebaptism. Immersion of a confessing believer is the norm; someone baptised before believing receives a first true baptism, not a repetition. Others: Many churches sprinkle or pour, and regard later baptism as rebaptism. (Where: Acts 8; Acts 19)

Baptism and salvation. Baptism does not regenerate; it is the God-given sign of union with Christ by faith, so closely tied to the reality that Scripture can speak of the sign as doing it. Others: Rome, Orthodoxy, Lutherans and some Anglicans hold that baptism conveys new birth. (Where: Acts 2; 1 Peter 3; Titus 3; Romans 6)

The Lord’s Supper. Christ is truly present by his Spirit and believers feed on him by faith, while the bread and wine remain what they are (the Reformed view); no frequency is commanded, though weekly communion is a blessing. Others: Transubstantiation, the Lutheran view, or a memorial only. (Where: The Church (The Lord’s Supper); 1 Corinthians 10–11; Matthew 26)

Who may come to the table. Baptised believers who trust Christ, are not under discipline and examine themselves, whatever their congregation; a long-professing member with dementia should not be turned away. Others: Some practise open communion, others closed. (Where: 1 Corinthians 11; Biblical Counseling (Hard Cases: Alzheimer’s))

Worship. The regulative principle, applied with wisdom: Scripture governs the elements of worship, while circumstances are ordered by wisdom; drama, liturgical dance and religious images are additions. Others: The normative principle allows whatever Scripture does not forbid. (Where: Worship & the Lord’s Day (Worshipping God His Way); John 4; Deuteronomy 12)

Images of Christ. No image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer, following the Reformed caution on the second commandment. Others: Many hold that because Christ took a real body he may be depicted; Orthodox and Catholics venerate icons and images. (Where: Deuteronomy 5)

Singing. The church may sing faithful hymns that name Christ, while the Psalms deserve a far larger place. Others: Some Reformed churches sing only the Psalms. (Where: Worship & the Lord’s Day (Singing to the Lord); Colossians 3)

The Lord’s Day. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and Sunday is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a law with rules about work; no one may bind another’s conscience. Others: Many godly brothers, with Westminster and 1689, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath; Adventists keep Saturday. (Where: Worship & the Lord’s Day (The Lord’s Day); The Ten Commandments; Colossians 2; Romans 14)

Church discipline. Discipline is commanded by Christ, carried out by the church under its elders in stages, and aims at restoration. Others: Many churches neglect it. (Where: 1 Corinthians 5; 2 Thessalonians 3)

One mediator. Confession is made to God through Christ alone; confessing to one another is good, but there is no priestly absolution and no praying to saints or angels. Others: Rome requires confession to a priest and invites the saints’ intercession. (Where: 1 John 1; John 20; Colossians 2; Hebrews 12)

Clerical celibacy. Ministers may marry, and requiring celibacy has no basis in Scripture; celibacy is a gift for some. Others: Rome requires celibacy of most priests. (Where: 1 Corinthians 9; 1 Timothy 4)

Elders’ qualifications. A man divorced on biblical grounds who has lived faithfully may be considered, and an elder’s children must be orderly and respectful, not necessarily converted. Others: Some bar every divorced man; some require all an elder’s children to be believers. (Where: 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1; Divorce & Remarriage (Remarriage and Grace))

Women in ministry. Complementarian: women pray, serve and teach in many settings, some prophesied in apostolic times, and Deborah and Huldah were prophets raised up by God, but the eldership and authoritative teaching in the gathered church belong to qualified men, grounded in creation. Others: Egalitarians open every ministry to men and women alike. (Where: 1 Timothy 2; 1 Corinthians 14; Acts 18; Romans 16; Judges 4; 2 Kings 22)

Women deacons. Either reading of 1 Timothy 3:11 is within faithful bounds, and women may serve in a diaconal role, as Phoebe probably did. Others: Some keep the diaconate for men only. (Where: 1 Timothy 3; Romans 16)

Head coverings. The creation principle of male and female and the husband’s headship is permanent; the head covering was its Corinthian form. Others: Some churches require head coverings today. (Where: 1 Corinthians 11)

Israel and the covenants

One people of God. One people of God across history under one covenant of grace: believing Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, and the Israel of God is all believers; fulfilment, not replacement. Others: Dispensationalists keep Israel and the church as two peoples; some speak of the church replacing Israel. (Where: Galatians 3; Galatians 6; Romans 11; 1 Peter 2; Covenant Theology)

The new covenant. All its members know the Lord, which is why its sign is given to those who believe; this commentary follows the 1689 Confession’s reading of the covenants as less continuous than Westminster’s. Others: Presbyterian and other paedobaptists read the covenants as more continuous and include believers’ children. (Where: Hebrews 8; Jeremiah 31; Denominations (Anabaptist & Mennonite))

The land and the kingdom. The land promise was fulfilled in Joshua’s day and points to the whole new earth, and the kingdom is restored as the Messiah reigns from heaven and gathers the nations now. Others: Dispensationalists expect the land and a political kingdom for national Israel in a future millennium. (Where: Genesis 12; Numbers 34; Joshua 1; Jeremiah 30; Ezekiel 11; Amos 9; Obadiah; Acts 1)

Israel today. The promise to bless those who bless Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, and the modern state of Israel is not the fulfilment of the land promises; Christians should love the Jewish people, beloved for the fathers’ sake, pray for their salvation and judge any nation by God’s justice. Others: Christian Zionists and many dispensationalists see the modern state as prophetic fulfilment. (Where: Genesis 12; Amos 9; Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 28)

All Israel will be saved. This commentary does not press one reading, but holds with humility that Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God. Others: Calvin read all Israel as the whole church; others as the elect remnant; dispensationalists add a separate national plan. (Where: Romans 11; Hermeneutics; Matthew 23)

A rebuilt temple. The New Testament never expects a rebuilt temple or renewed sacrifice; Ezekiel’s closing temple vision is a picture fulfilled in Christ, his church and the new Jerusalem. Others: Many dispensationalists expect a future temple with memorial sacrifices. (Where: 2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 11; Ezekiel, Introduction; Ezekiel 48; Jeremiah 33)

Old Testament kingdom prophecies. Promises of Zion exalted, David’s throne, peace among the nations and Jerusalem rescued are read with the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ’s present reign and the gospel, and completed in the new creation; Jerusalem besieged in Zechariah stands for God’s people assaulted to the end. Others: Premillennial and dispensational readers expect a literal earthly kingdom centred on Jerusalem. (Where: Isaiah 2, 9, 11, 35, 65; Micah 4; Zechariah 12, 14; 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17; Psalm 89)

The law. Israel’s civil and ceremonial laws are fulfilled and ended; the moral law remains the rule of life, as the shape of love, not a way to earn salvation. Others: Theonomists would apply Israel’s civil laws today; New Covenant Theology sees the law replaced by the law of Christ. (Where: Matthew 5; 1 Timothy 1; Galatians 3)

Food laws and customs. All foods are clean, and the Acts 15 rules served fellowship at that time; Jewish believers were free to keep customs as devotion, never as the way of salvation. Others: Adventists and some Messianic Jews keep the food laws. (Where: Acts 10; Acts 15; Acts 21)

The conquest and Amalek. These were God’s unique judgements on persistent wickedness, never a pattern or licence for violence today. Others: Critics see ethnic hostility. (Where: Genesis 15; Exodus 17)

The last things

The millennium. Amillennial: the thousand years are the present age, in which Christ reigns from heaven, the dead in Christ reign with him, and Satan, bound at the cross, cannot stop the gospel. Others: Premillennialists expect an earthly reign after Christ returns; postmillennialists a golden age before it. (Where: Revelation 20; End Times Models; Matthew 12; Matthew 13)

One return, no secret rapture. Christ returns once, visibly and bodily, after the tribulation, and believers are caught up to meet him then; in Luke 17 those taken are taken in judgement, and Revelation 3:10 means protection within trial. Others: Dispensationalists teach a secret rapture seven years before his visible coming. (Where: 1 Thessalonians 4; Matthew 24; Luke 17; Revelation 3; The Person & Work of Christ (He Will Come Again))

Resurrection and judgement. One general resurrection of the just and the unjust at Christ’s return, then one judgement and the new creation. Others: Premillennialists see two resurrections separated by the millennium. (Where: Revelation 20; Acts 24; 2 Peter 3)

The last days and the tribulation. The last days are the whole church age since Pentecost, and the great tribulation is the suffering of God’s people through it, rising to a final intensity. Others: Dispensationalists place both in a short future period, with a seven-year tribulation. (Where: Acts 2; 2 Timothy 3; Revelation 7; Daniel 12)

The Olivet Discourse. Matthew 24:4–35 and Mark 13 speak mainly of the events up to AD 70, which foreshadow the end, then of Christ’s return; this generation means Jesus’ contemporaries. Others: Futurists apply most of it to a final tribulation; some critics say Jesus was mistaken. (Where: Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 21)

The man of lawlessness. A final individual opponent destroyed at Christ’s coming, while the spirit of antichrist works throughout the age; the restrainer is most likely God’s providence through government and law. Others: Others see a principle only, or (as many Reformers did) the papacy; some say the restrainer is the Spirit removed at a rapture. (Where: 2 Thessalonians 2; 1 John 2; The Bible Book by Book (2 Thessalonians))

The beast, the mark and 666. The beast is the persecuting state or system that claims divine honours, first Rome; the mark is a symbol of allegiance, not a device; 666 pointed first to Nero. Others: Historicists saw the papacy; futurists expect a single world dictator; many tie 666 to recent figures or technology. (Where: Revelation 13)

Reading Revelation. It spoke first to first-century churches, then in repeated cycles pictures the conflict of the whole age, ending in Christ’s return. Others: Preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist readings each stress one aspect. (Where: Revelation 1)

Date-setting. Scripture gives no timetable and forbids date-setting; the return is near as the next great event. Others: Some calculate dates, such as six thousand years of history. (Where: 2 Peter 3; Luke 21)

The intermediate state. At death believers go immediately and consciously to be with Christ; there is no soul sleep, and the rich man and Lazarus, though a parable, teaches conscious existence after death. Others: Some teach soul sleep until the resurrection. (Where: Death, Dying & Heaven (What Happens When We Die?); Philippians 1; Luke 16; Revelation 6)

Purgatory. There is no purgatory and no warrant for prayers for the dead; Christ’s single offering has perfected his people. Others: Rome teaches purifying suffering after death. (Where: Death, Dying & Heaven; 1 Corinthians 3; 2 Timothy 1; Luke 23)

Hell. Hell is conscious, eternal punishment: Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence. Others: Some evangelicals, such as John Stott tentatively, hold that the lost are finally destroyed. (Where: The Attributes of God (Righteous and Wrathful); Matthew 25; Mark 9; Revelation 14)

The new creation. This creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Others: Some expect it destroyed and replaced, or a purely spiritual heaven. (Where: Revelation 21; Romans 8)

Christian life

Sanctification. God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work because he works; the old self was put off at conversion and must be lived out; perfection is never reached here, and passivity is never commanded. Others: Perfectionism; higher-life teaching (let go and let God); effort with little grace. (Where: Fighting Sin & Temptation (Putting Sin to Death); Philippians 2; Ephesians 4; Matthew 5)

Romans 7. Romans 7:14–25 describes Paul as a believer, the honest struggle of every Christian, answered by Romans 8. Others: Many read it as Paul before conversion. (Where: Fighting Sin & Temptation (Why Christians Still Sin); Romans 7)

Temptation and sin. Being tempted is not sin; the remaining fallen nature is sin we fight and grieve over, without condemnation; consenting to temptation is sin needing repentance. Others: Some treat temptation as sin; others deny the remaining corruption is sin. (Where: Ephesians 5)

Law and liberty. The moral law has three uses (to show sin, restrain evil and guide believers); where Scripture is silent believers are free, and human rules made a test of holiness become self-made religion. Others: Some fear any law for believers; some churches bind rules such as no alcohol or dancing. (Where: 1 Timothy 1; Romans 14; Colossians 2)

Spiritual warfare. Satan is real but acts only within God’s permission; the weapons are the ordinary means of grace, not techniques for binding territorial spirits. Others: Some deliverance ministries map and bind spirits; scepticism neglects the battle. (Where: Ephesians 6; 2 Corinthians 10; 1 Thessalonians 2)

Demons and believers. A true believer cannot be possessed by a demon, though he can be tempted and attacked. Others: Some teach that believers can be demonised and need deliverance. (Where: Spiritual Warfare (Standing Firm))

Suffering and prosperity. Suffering is normal for Christians; God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich or always healthy. Others: The prosperity gospel promises health and wealth to faith. (Where: 1 Timothy 6; 3 John; 2 Corinthians 4; Philippians 4)

Anxiety. Believers must not be ruled by anxiety, and the remedy is prayer with thanksgiving, but feeling anxious is not in itself sin. Others: Some say all anxiety shows lack of faith. (Where: Philippians 4)

Forgiveness. In the heart we let go of bitterness whether or not the other repents; the restored relationship waits for repentance. Others: Some hold forgiveness complete only on repentance. (Where: Ephesians 4)

Truthfulness and oaths. The sources differ here: Colossians 3 and Hebrews 11 hold that every lie is a sin, though extreme cases are rare and godly believers differ, and praise Rahab’s faith, not her lie; Joshua 2 judges it more likely that deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. Casual oaths are forbidden; lawful oaths are permitted. Others: Augustine and Calvin held every lie a sin; many hold that hiding the innocent from murderers by deception is right; Quakers and Anabaptists refuse all oaths. (Where: Colossians 3; Hebrews 11; Joshua 2; Exodus 1; Matthew 5)

Apologetics. No thought is neutral: reason carefully and use evidence, but from submission to God’s revelation, bringing philosophy captive to Christ. Others: Some seek neutral common ground; some think all philosophy is forbidden. (Where: 2 Corinthians 10; Colossians 2)

Biblical counselling. Scripture is sufficient for the care of souls: our deepest problem is always spiritual, yet the body matters, so depression calls for a medical check alongside counselling, psychiatric care and medication have their place, and much depression is suffering, not sin. Others: Many integrate secular psychology as an equal authority; some treat all depression as a spiritual failing. (Where: Biblical Counseling (The Sufficiency of Scripture; Depression; Severe Mental Illness))

Suicide. Suicide is a grave sin, the taking of a life that belongs to God, but a person in crisis needs care, presence and hope first; active intent means acting at once and calling the emergency services. Others: Some have taught that suicide cannot be forgiven. (Where: Biblical Counseling (Hard Cases: Suicide and Self-Harm); Luke 12)

Technology. Technology is a tool under God, to be used with wisdom and gratitude, neither feared nor embraced uncritically; screens become idols when we turn to them for what only God gives, and pornography is adultery of the heart that enslaves. Others: Some Christians fear all new technology; others embrace it uncritically. (Where: Technology & the Christian Mind (Tools and the Heart; Mastered by Nothing))

Marriage, sexuality and family

Marriage. The lifelong union of one man and one woman, the only place for sexual union, a living parable of Christ and the church, but not a sacrament. Others: Some churches affirm same-sex marriage; Rome counts marriage a sacrament. (Where: Ephesians 5; Hebrews 13)

Headship and submission. Complementarian: equal in worth, different by design; head means authority exercised as Christ exercises it, in self-giving love, grounded in creation; Galatians 3:28 concerns status, not roles. Others: Egalitarians hold mutual submission without distinct roles. (Where: Genesis 2; Ephesians 5; 1 Peter 3; Galatians 3)

Abuse. Abuse is never tolerated: the abused should seek safety at once, abuse must be reported, and leaving to escape it is not the separation Paul forbids. Others: Some have counselled victims to stay and submit. (Where: Divorce & Remarriage (Abuse, Separation and Hard Cases); Christian Marriage; Ezekiel 16)

Grounds for divorce. Only adultery or desertion (Westminster 24.5–6); persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, and the elders help judge each case. Others: Some allow no divorce, some adultery only, some many reasons. (Where: Divorce & Remarriage (Grounds for Divorce); Matthew 19; Mark 10; Ephesians 5; Deuteronomy 24; Hosea 3)

Remarriage. The innocent party may remarry; those already remarried should not leave their present marriage but repent of any wrong in how it began. Others: Some forbid remarriage while a former spouse lives. (Where: Divorce & Remarriage (Remarriage and Grace); 1 Corinthians 7; Malachi 2)

Singleness. Singleness and marriage are both gifts, and neither is holier. Others: Rome has prized celibacy as higher; some church culture treats singleness as second best. (Where: 1 Corinthians 7; Ephesians 5)

Same-sex relationships. The historic view, held with compassion: same-sex sexual relationships are contrary to God’s will, since the texts rest on creation, not on exploitation. Others: Some say the texts address only exploitation and affirm committed partnerships. (Where: Biblical Sexuality (Same-Sex Attraction); Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 6)

Sex and gender. God gives our sex through our bodies, and altering the body to deny it rejects his design; compassion must govern how we speak and act. Others: Some hold that inner identity determines sex and support medical transition. (Where: Biblical Sexuality (Male and Female He Created Them))

Family planning. Onan’s sin was refusing his duty to his brother’s widow, not contraception; Christians may differ on family planning while welcoming children. Others: Rome has cited Onan against contraception. (Where: Genesis 38)

Discipline of children. The rod passages most likely permitted measured physical discipline of young children, given calmly and in love; discipline that frightens, injures or humiliates is abuse. Others: Others read the rod figuratively, and some think physical discipline always unwise. (Where: Biblical Wisdom (Passing Wisdom On); Ephesians 6)

Children of believers. Believing parents are a great gift, and their children are set apart by that relation, but this does not qualify them for baptism. Others: Paedobaptists see covenant holiness as grounds for infant baptism. (Where: 1 Corinthians 7; 2 Timothy 1; Luke 18)

Saved through childbearing. 1 Timothy 2:15 most likely means women live out their salvation in their calling, motherhood included, perhaps also pointing to Christ’s birth; salvation is by grace through faith. Others: Others read kept safe in childbirth, or saved through the birth of the Child. (Where: Biblical Womanhood (Eve, the Fall and the Promised Offspring))

The Song of Songs. Its first meaning is plain: the love of husband and wife, physical delight included, heard with the echo of Christ and his church that all marriage carries. Others: Jewish teachers, many fathers, Bernard and many Puritans read it chiefly as allegory. (Where: Song of Songs, Introduction)

Ethics and society

The sanctity of life. Every human being, from the smallest embryo to the oldest adult, bears God’s image, and worth depends on God, not on ability, health or being wanted; Scripture forbids the deliberate killing of the innocent, while permitting just punishment by the state and self-defence. Others: Some thinkers grant full rights only to those with abilities such as self-awareness. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (The Sanctity of Human Life))

Abortion. Unborn children are human persons, so deliberately ending their lives is forbidden by the sixth commandment; Exodus 21:22–25 most naturally describes a premature birth, and there is full forgiveness in Christ for those involved. Others: Some read Exodus 21 as a miscarriage valued less than a life, and many hold abortion permissible. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (Life Before Birth))

Hard cases in pregnancy. A child conceived in rape is still an innocent life, and the mother needs enormous support; where the pregnancy directly threatens the mother’s life, as in an ectopic pregnancy, treating her to save her life is not deliberate killing and is permitted. Others: Many allow abortion in cases of rape or serious disability. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (Life Before Birth))

IVF and embryos. The middle position is wise: IVF within marriage with the couple’s own eggs and sperm is permissible if every embryo is treated as a child, creating only as many as will be implanted, destroying none, and avoiding donor gametes and surrogacy; existing frozen embryos may be adopted. Others: Some Christians reject IVF entirely; others accept it freely, treating embryos as potential life. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (Infertility, IVF and Embryos))

Disability and prenatal testing. No life is a mistake: people with disabilities are image-bearers and indispensable members of the church; testing may help families prepare, but should never lead to aborting a child for a diagnosis. Others: In many places testing routinely leads to abortion. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (Disability and the Value of Every Life))

Euthanasia and assisted suicide. Both are forbidden, even when motivated by compassion, because life belongs to God; they also press the weak to feel they are a burden. Others: Some argue that suffering people should be helped to die. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (The End of Life); Death, Dying & Heaven (Preparing to Die Well))

Treatment at the end of life. The line is between allowing death and causing it: Christians may decline or withdraw burdensome treatment with little hope and give good pain relief even if it may shorten life; excellent palliative care and making one’s wishes known are wise. Others: Some hold that every possible treatment must always be pursued. (Where: Life & Death Ethics (The End of Life))

Capital punishment. The state may punish the gravest crimes, such as murder, with death, exercised justly and with great care. Others: Some Christians hold it always wrong, from mercy and the risk of error. (Where: Genesis 9; Romans 13; Acts 25)

Obeying the state. Submit to authorities in all lawful things, even unjust rulers; where the state commands sin or forbids obedience to God, obey God openly and peacefully and accept the consequences. Others: Some say always obey; others that any unjust law may be resisted. (Where: Romans 13; 1 Peter 2; Acts 4)

Resistance. Private believers may never take up the sword against government, but may use courts, elections, petitions and peaceful protest; lawful authorities may have a duty to restrain a tyrant. Others: A Reformed strand lets lesser magistrates resist tyrants; some justify revolution. (Where: The Christian & the World (When We Must Obey God Rather than Men))

The church and politics. The church preaches the gospel and Christ’s whole moral law, which has public implications, but its pulpits should not endorse parties or candidates, and on policy questions such as tax, healthcare or immigration levels faithful Christians may disagree; Christians pay taxes and give ultimate loyalty to God alone. Others: Some want the church to campaign; others want it silent; theonomists would base civil law on Israel’s. (Where: The Christian & the World (Christians and Politics); Matthew 22)

War and force. Jesus forbids personal revenge, not the state’s lawful force, service as soldiers or police, or defending the vulnerable; Christ’s kingdom itself is never advanced by the sword or coercion. Others: Pacifists (Anabaptists, Quakers) refuse all force, and are to be respected. (Where: Matthew 5; Luke 6; Romans 12; John 18; 2 Kings 3; Life & Death Ethics (The Sanctity of Human Life))

Lawsuits. Settle disputes between believers within the church, and often accept loss, though legal protection may be needed where someone refuses correction. Others: Some say never sue; others treat the courts as open to all. (Where: 1 Corinthians 6)

Slavery. The New Testament regulated an institution it did not create while planting principles that undermined it; Wilberforce rightly led abolition, and trafficking must be opposed. Others: Some say the New Testament approved slavery. (Where: 1 Corinthians 7; 1 Timothy 6; Ephesians 6; Philemon)

Giving and tithing. No fixed percentage is commanded, but regular, proportionate, generous, cheerful giving; the tithe is a helpful benchmark, and many should give more. Others: Some bind Christians to exactly a tenth. (Where: 1 Corinthians 16; Luke 11; Hebrews 7)

Property, sharing and debt. The sharing in Acts was voluntary love, not a compulsory system or state redistribution; borrowing is not forbidden, but unnecessary debt is unwise, and commercial interest is lawful while exploiting the poor through it is wrong; care for the poor is not optional. Others: Some see a model for Christian communism; some forbid all loans or all interest. (Where: Acts 2; 2 Corinthians 8; Romans 13; Money & Stewardship (Debt, Work, and Integrity; Justice and the Poor); Leading a Business for Christ (Bankers, Investors, Lawyers and Regulators))

Business and profit. Profit is necessary but not the goal; a Christian business should not make money from harmful products such as pornography, predatory loans or addictive gambling, should pay suppliers promptly, refuse bribes, and pay its tax in the spirit of the law, not through schemes whose only purpose is avoidance. Others: Some treat business as a necessary evil or merely a platform for evangelism; others see aggressive tax avoidance as simply good stewardship. (Where: Leading a Business for Christ (Why Business Matters to God; Customers; Suppliers and Partners; Competitors, Government and Money))

Work and vocation. Every honest calling is service to God; the split between sacred and secular work that the Reformers rejected is wrong, and integrity in work is part of our witness. Others: Many treat only church work as truly spiritual. (Where: Christian at Work (Vocation and Calling); Leading a Business for Christ)

Alcohol. Wine is God’s gift and Jesus made real wine; moderate drinking is Christian liberty, drunkenness is forbidden, and love gladly abstains for a weaker brother. Others: Some argue biblical wine was unfermented and require abstinence. (Where: John 2; Romans 14)

Sunday work and trading. Opening or closing on Sunday can both be done in good faith, but staff must have real rest and freedom to worship. Others: Those holding the Sabbath view close as a testimony. (Where: Leading a Business for Christ (Competitors, Government and Money))

Interpretation of particular passages

The sons of God (Genesis 6). Genesis 6 leaves the question genuinely hard, weighing the angel and Sethite views; 1 Peter 3 calls the angel reading the more likely, held without dogmatism. Others: Fallen angels, the line of Seth (Calvin), or tyrant kings. (Where: Genesis 6; 1 Peter 3)

Genesis 3:15–16. The offspring of 3:15 points to Christ, not Mary; the woman’s desire in 3:16 is a sinful struggle for control answered by harsh rule, a curse Christ came to undo. Others: Marian readings of 3:15; reading 3:16 as romantic longing. (Where: Genesis 3)

Melchizedek. A real, historical king-priest whose life God arranged to foreshadow Christ; his bread and wine were a meal, not a sacrifice. Others: A pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, or an angel; Rome sees the Mass prefigured. (Where: Genesis 14; Hebrews 7)

Abraham and Isaac. God, the giver of life, had the right to require it, never meant it to happen, and later forbade child sacrifice absolutely. Others: Kierkegaard saw faith suspending ethics. (Where: Genesis 22)

The exodus. A real event; Exodus 1 leaves the date open, while the Introduction takes the early date (about 1446 BC) as the better reading; the large numbers are the plain reading, and the plagues, crossing and manna were miraculous. Others: Smaller numbers (elef as clan); natural explanations. (Where: Exodus, Introduction; Exodus 1; Exodus 7; Exodus 12; Exodus 16; Numbers 1)

Job’s friends. Their speeches must never be quoted as God’s verdict on a sufferer, for God said they had not spoken rightly of him. Others: Many quote them as straightforward teaching. (Where: Job 4; Job 42)

Elihu. Elihu speaks partly truly and partly not, and the book gives no verdict on him. Others: Some see him as God’s spokesman, others as another mistaken friend. (Where: Job 32; Job 42)

Isaiah 7:14. A child born in those years was the near sign, and the prophecy reached beyond him to Immanuel himself, as Matthew says. Others: Some see only a direct prediction of Christ; critics see only a child of Isaiah’s day. (Where: Isaiah 7)

Lucifer and the king of Tyre. Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 are about human kings, whose pride mirrors the pride of the devil behind them. Others: Many read them as direct accounts of Satan’s fall. (Where: Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 28)

Isaiah 53. The servant is an individual, Christ, suffering for the people and distinct from them. Others: Jewish interpretation often reads the servant as Israel. (Where: Isaiah 53)

Daniel’s seventy weeks. Daniel 9:24–27 is fulfilled in Christ’s first coming and Jerusalem’s fall, with no gap the text does not mention. Others: Dispensationalists place a gap before a final week; critics apply it to the 160s BC. (Where: Daniel 9)

Daniel 11 and the numbers. Daniel 11:40–45 looks beyond Antiochus to the final enemy, and the three and a half times are symbolic. Others: Critical scholars keep the verses about Antiochus; many read literal years. (Where: Daniel 7; Daniel 11)

Psalm 82’s gods. Israel’s human judges, holding God’s authority. Others: Some see heavenly powers over the nations. (Where: John 10)

Water and Spirit. In John 3:5 water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, as in Ezekiel 36, not baptism. Others: Baptism, physical birth, or John’s baptism. (Where: John 3)

The Sermon on the Mount. Christ’s teaching for his disciples now: it humbles, drives to grace and shapes the forgiven. Others: Some confine it to a future kingdom. (Where: Matthew 5)

Some standing here. The transfiguration was the first fulfilment of Matthew 16:28 and Mark 9:1, with the resurrection and enthronement the full reality. Others: AD 70 or Pentecost; critics say Jesus expected the end in his lifetime. (Where: Mark 9; Matthew 16; compare Matthew 10)

Hebrews 6. Those described had tasted the blessings of the gospel community without being regenerate; their falling away shows they were never saved. Others: Believers losing salvation; a hypothetical warning; loss of rewards. (Where: Hebrews 6)

The least of these. In Matthew 25 they are most likely Christ’s needy disciples, though Scripture commands care for all the poor. Others: Many read all the poor and suffering. (Where: Matthew 25)

The 144,000. The whole church, the true Israel of God, sealed on earth; the great multitude is the same church before the throne, and the twenty-four elders are the whole people of God. Others: Jewish believers in a future tribulation; a special class (Jehovah’s Witnesses). (Where: Revelation 7; Revelation 4)

Revelation 11 and 12. The measured temple and the two witnesses are the church and its witness through the age, and the woman is the people of God, with a secondary allusion to Mary. Others: Futurists expect a rebuilt temple and two prophets; Rome sees Mary in the woman. (Where: Revelation 11; Revelation 12)

Babylon and Armageddon. Babylon is Rome in John’s day, standing for the seductive world system of every age; Armageddon is a symbolic name for the final conflict, and Gog and Magog in Ezekiel 38–39 and Revelation 20 are the nations gathered for the last assault on the church, not Russia. Others: Many Reformers saw the papacy in Babylon; popular teachers map Armageddon and Gog literally. (Where: Revelation 16; Revelation 17; Revelation 20; Ezekiel 38)
